title: Melting and freezing
keyIdea: Warming makes ice melt into water. Cooling makes water freeze into ice. Ice is a solid: it keeps its shape. Water is a liquid: it flows and takes the shape of its cup. The warmer the place, the faster ice melts, and melted ice can freeze again, so this change goes both ways.

kid: Ice is hard. You can hold an ice cube. Ice is a solid.
Put the ice in a warm, sunny spot. It gets wet. It gets small. Soon it is a puddle of water. That is melting.
Water is runny. It flows. Put a cup of water in the freezer. The freezer is very cold. Later the water is hard ice. That is freezing.
The puddle can turn back into ice. Just make it very cold again. Warm melts. Cold freezes.
adult: This sits in early science under the natural world. The EYFS early learning goal asks children to understand changes in the natural world, including changing states of matter, and Development Matters for 3 and 4 year olds asks them to talk about the changes they notice in materials. NGSS K-PS3-1 has kindergartners observe how sunlight warms things, and the Head Start ELOF asks children to observe and describe changes in materials. The habit is the same: predict, try it, and look again later.

Key words for this age are solid, liquid, melt, freeze, warm (heat) and cool. A solid keeps its shape; a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. Melting is solid to liquid when something warms up; freezing is liquid to solid when it cools down. Water freezes at 0 °C, which is why a home freezer (about −18 °C) works and a fridge (about 4 °C) does not. Melting and freezing can be undone, unlike cooking an egg; NGSS returns to this in grade 2 (2-PS1-4).

Common mistakes: thinking ice disappears when it melts, when the water is still there in the puddle; thinking heat makes ice harder; thinking a fridge will make ice; and thinking melted ice can never be ice again. Children also say the sun melts things only by shining on them, so be careful to name warmth: a warm room melts ice too, just more slowly.

In the lab your child drags an ice cube to the sunny window, the table or the freezer and watches what happens, freezes cups of water, races three ice lollies in the three places, freezes a puddle back into ice and melts it again, and then picks warm or cold to do kitchen jobs. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Put one ice cube on a plate by a sunny window and one on a plate in a cool room. Ask 'Which will melt first?' Check every few minutes. Then pour the water back into the tray, freeze it, and look again in the morning.

visual.caption: Does it melt or freeze? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: melt ice in the sun, freeze water in the freezer, race three ice lollies, turn a puddle back into ice, and pick warm or cold for kitchen jobs.

practice.prompt: Melting and freezing: an ice cube sits in a warm, sunny window. What happens?
practice.hint: Think of an ice lolly on a hot day. What does warm do to ice?
practice.explain: Warm makes ice melt. The hard ice turns into runny water, and you can see a puddle.

practice.prompt: There are {n} ice cubes in the freezer. You take 2 out and put them in the sun. How many ice cubes stay hard in the freezer?
practice.hint: The freezer keeps ice hard. Only the 2 in the sun melt. Take 2 away from {n}.
practice.explain: {n} take away 2 is {=n-2}. Those {=n-2} stay hard because the freezer is very cold.

practice.prompt: You want to make ice cubes. Where do you put the tray of water?
practice.hint: Water needs to get very, very cold to turn into ice.
practice.explain: The freezer is very cold, so the water freezes into hard ice cubes. The window and table are too warm.

practice.prompt: One tray makes {n} ice cubes. You fill 2 trays and put them in the freezer. How many ice cubes do you get?
practice.hint: Each tray makes {n}. Count {n}, then count on {n} more.
practice.explain: {n} and {n} more make {=2*n} ice cubes, once the water has frozen.

choices: The one in the hot sun
pool.hint: The warmest place melts ice the fastest.
pool.explain: The hot sun is the warmest place, so that ice lolly melts first. The freezer keeps its lolly hard.

pool.prompt: An ice cube melts on a plate. Where did the ice go?
choices: It is the water on the plate
It went back to the freezer
pool.hint: Look at the plate. Is it dry or wet?
pool.explain: The ice did not vanish. It melted, and the water on the plate is the same stuff, now runny.

pool.prompt: A puddle of melted ice goes in the freezer. What happens?
pool.hint: In the lab, the puddle went in the freezer. What did it turn into?
pool.explain: Very cold turns water back into ice. Melting and freezing go both ways.

pool.hint: A solid keeps its shape. You can pick it up.
pool.explain: An ice cube keeps its shape, so it is a solid. Water and juice flow, so they are liquids.

pool.prompt: You have {n} ice lollies. You leave 1 in the sun and it melts. How many are still hard?
pool.hint: Only the one in the sun melted. Take 1 away from {n}.
pool.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. The other {=n-1} stayed hard in the cold.

pool.hint: Snow is frozen water. What makes frozen water melt?
pool.explain: Snow melts when the air gets warm. Cold weather keeps a snowman hard.

pool.prompt: You want to melt butter for a cake. What do you need?
pool.hint: Melting makes hard things soft and runny. Does warm or cold do that?
pool.explain: Warm melts butter. Cold, like a freezer, would keep the butter hard.

pool.prompt: Water is runny and flows. What do we call it when water turns into hard ice?
pool.hint: Melting makes ice runny. The other way round has a different name.
pool.explain: Water turning into ice is freezing. Ice turning into water is melting.

pool.prompt: You leave {n} ice cubes in the hot sun and {n} ice cubes in the freezer. Later, how many ice cubes are still hard?
pool.hint: Which place keeps ice hard? Which place melts it? Count only the hard ones.
pool.explain: The {n} in the sun melted into water. The {n} in the freezer stayed hard, so {n} are still hard.
